# nish/threads

Data parallelism, a scope for heterogeneous tasks, and a lock that owns its data (docs/wp29-thread-surface.md §4.1, §4.2 and §4.3).

```ts
import {
  AtomicI32,
  AtomicI64,
  Channel,
  Mutex,
  MutexGuard,
  ThreadScope,
  parallelFrom,
  parallelMap,
  parallelMapInto,
  parallelReduce,
  scope,
  scopeWithStack,
} from "nish/threads";
```

<scalar-code-group>

```ts example.ts
import { parallelFrom, parallelMap, parallelMapInto, parallelReduce, scope, scopeWithStack } from "nish/threads";

const sumOf = (xs: i32[]): i32 => {
  let total: i32 = 0;
  for (const x of xs) {
    total = total + x;
  }
  return total;
};

export const main = (): i32 => {
  const src: i32[] = [1, 2, 3, 4];
  const k: i32 = 10;
  const dst: i32[] = [0, 0, 0, 0];
  parallelMapInto(src, dst, (x) => x * 3);               // dst is [3, 6, 9, 12]
  const ys = parallelMap(src, (x) => x * k);             // [10, 20, 30, 40]: `k` is read by the body
  const sq = parallelFrom(4, (i) => i * i);              // [0, 1, 4, 9]
  const total = parallelReduce(src, (a, b) => a + b, 0); // 10
  const out: i32[] = [0, 0];
  {
    using s = scope();
    s.spawn(sumOf, ys, out, 0);
    s.spawn(sumOf, sq, out, 1);
  } // both tasks have run, and `out` is [100, 14]
  {
    using s = scopeWithStack(64 * 1024 * 1024); // each task's thread has a 64 MiB stack
    s.spawn(sumOf, src, out, 0);
  }
  return total;
};
```

</scalar-code-group>

<scalar-grid cols="2">

<scalar-card title="parallel​From" icon="phosphor/regular/function" href="#parallelfrom">

A new array of `n` elements, `f(i)` at index `i`, computed on as many threads as the machine has and the length is worth: `Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => f(i))`, with the array allocated before any element is.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="parallel​Map" icon="phosphor/regular/function" href="#parallelmap">

A new array of `f(src[i])` for every index of `src`: `parallelMapInto` into an array this call allocates, before any element is computed, so nothing but the map itself can hold it while the region runs.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="parallel​Map​Into" icon="phosphor/regular/function" href="#parallelmapinto">

`dst[i] = f(src[i])` for every index of `src`, on as many threads as the machine has and the length is worth.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="parallel​Reduce" icon="phosphor/regular/function" href="#parallelreduce">

`f` folded over `src`, blockwise from `identity` and then left to right over the blocks, so the answer does not depend on how many threads computed it.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="scope" icon="phosphor/regular/function" href="#scope">

A new scope, for a `using` declaration: `using s = scope()`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="scope​With​Stack" icon="phosphor/regular/function" href="#scopewithstack">

A new scope whose tasks each run on a thread with a stack of at least `bytes` bytes, for a `using` declaration: `using s = scopeWithStack(n)`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="Atomic​I32" icon="phosphor/regular/cube" href="#atomici32">

An `i32` that a scope's tasks and a parallel body may update together (docs/LANGUAGE.md, "Atomics").

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="Atomic​I64" icon="phosphor/regular/cube" href="#atomici64">

An `i64` that a scope's tasks and a parallel body may update together (docs/LANGUAGE.md, "Atomics").

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="Channel" icon="phosphor/regular/cube" href="#channel">

A channel of scalars or strings between a scope's tasks (docs/wp29-thread-surface.md §4.4); a string is copied out of the sender's arena at `send` and into the receiver's at the loop: `send` from the tasks that produce, `for (const x of ch)` in the one that consumes, or in the parent once the scope has joined.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="Mutex" icon="phosphor/regular/cube" href="#mutex">

</scalar-card>

What a `Mutex` hands out: its data, as `value`, for as long as the block of the `using` declaration that took the lock (docs/LANGUAGE.md, "A lock that owns its data").

<scalar-detail title="What is written here is the meaning, not the implementation">

Each body
below is the sequential program, and it is what runs under Node, what `npm
run check` type-checks, and what the compiler checks the call against.

The compiler then recognises the exported templates by module and name and
lowers an instance of `parallelMapInto`, `parallelFrom` or `parallelReduce`
onto `nish_parallel_range` (runtime/runtime-parallel.c): it replaces the one
call that walks the whole range — `mapRange` for a map, `fromRange` for a
`parallelFrom`, `reduceBlocks` for a reduce — with a region that hands each
thread a contiguous piece of it, and emits the rest of the body as written.
`parallelMap` is `parallelMapInto` into an array it allocates first. So the
length check, its message and the order a reduce combines in are this file's,
whichever way the program is compiled.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="What makes the region safe is checked at the call, not trusted">

**What makes the region safe is checked at the call, not trusted**
(docs/LANGUAGE.md, "Data parallelism"): the function passed as `f` may write
nothing its caller could observe, may allocate only temporaries it drops
before it returns — they are given back after every element — `dst` may not
be reachable from an element of `src`, and the result type is a number, a
`boolean` or an enum — or, for a map, a `string` or an array of those
scalars, which the join copies out of the worker's arena.

An arrow written at the call may read the `const` locals and the parameters
of the function it is written in: each one is handed to the body as a
parameter of its own, which no body may write through. Importing this module
compiles the program with `--threads`, because every worker needs an arena of
its own.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="A reduce is deterministic">

`src` is split into `min(64, ceil(n / BLOCK))`
blocks, each block is folded from `identity`, and the block results are
combined left to right — here, on one thread, and by the compiled program on
any number of them — so an `f64` sum is the same bits on one core or sixty
four. That needs `f` to be associative and `identity` to be its identity,
which the checker enforces for an arrow whose body is one operator on its two
parameters and cannot see through a named function.

</scalar-detail>

## Functions

### parallelFrom

A new array of `n` elements, `f(i)` at index `i`, computed on as many
threads as the machine has and the length is worth: `Array.from({ length:
n }, (_, i) => f(i))`, with the array allocated before any element is.

```ts
function parallelFrom<U>(
  n: i32,
  f: (i: i32) => U,
): U[]
```

<scalar-field name="n" type="i32" required>

how many elements the array has.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="f" type="(i: i32) =&gt; U" required>

computes the element at an index from the index alone, under the
  rules `parallelMapInto` gives its `f`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="U[]">

a new array of `n` elements, which the caller owns.

</scalar-field>

### parallelMap

A new array of `f(src[i])` for every index of `src`: `parallelMapInto` into
an array this call allocates, before any element is computed, so nothing
but the map itself can hold it while the region runs.

```ts
function parallelMap<T, U>(
  src: T[],
  f: (x: T) => U,
): U[]
```

<scalar-field name="src" type="T[]" required>

the elements to map, read and not written.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="f" type="(x: T) =&gt; U" required>

computes one element from one element of `src`, under the rules
  `parallelMapInto` gives its `f`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="U[]">

a new array of `src.length` elements, which the caller owns.

</scalar-field>

### parallelMapInto

`dst[i] = f(src[i])` for every index of `src`, on as many threads as the
machine has and the length is worth. `dst` must be at least as long as
`src`, which is checked once, before any element is written.

```ts
function parallelMapInto<T, U>(
  src: T[],
  dst: U[],
  f: (x: T) => U,
): void
```

<scalar-field name="src" type="T[]" required>

the elements to map, read and not written.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="dst" type="U[]" required>

where `f(src[i])` is written, at the same index. If it is shorter
  than `src` the program stops before any element is written; any elements
  past `src.length` are left as they were.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="f" type="(x: T) =&gt; U" required>

computes one element from one element of `src`. It is called once
  per element, natively on any thread and in no set order, so it may write
  nothing its caller could observe (see the module header).

</scalar-field>

### parallelReduce

`f` folded over `src`, blockwise from `identity` and then left to right over
the blocks, so the answer does not depend on how many threads computed it.
An empty `src` answers `identity`.

```ts
function parallelReduce<T>(
  src: T[],
  f: (acc: T, x: T) => T,
  identity: T,
): T
```

<scalar-field name="src" type="T[]" required>

the elements to fold, read and not written.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="f" type="(acc: T, x: T) =&gt; T" required>

combines an accumulator with an element, and the blocks' results
  with each other, so it must be associative for the answer to mean the
  fold it reads as.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="identity" type="T" required>

what each block's fold starts from, which must be `f`'s
  identity, such as `0` for `+`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="T">

the fold of every element of `src`, the same however many threads
  computed it.

</scalar-field>

### scope

A new scope, for a `using` declaration: `using s = scope()`.

```ts
function scope(): ThreadScope
```

<scalar-field name="returns" type="ThreadScope">

a new scope of its own, whose tasks run on threads of the
  platform's default stack size and are joined when the block ends.

</scalar-field>

### scopeWithStack

A new scope whose tasks each run on a thread with a stack of at least
`bytes` bytes, for a `using` declaration: `using s = scopeWithStack(n)`.
The tasks run on new threads, never on the one that joins. The runtime
rounds `bytes` up to the page size and adds a guard page below it, so a task
that overflows it faults instead of writing past it. Under Node, and on a
target without threads, the size is checked and has no other effect.

```ts
function scopeWithStack(bytes: i32): ThreadScope
```

<scalar-field name="bytes" type="i32" required>

the least stack each task's thread gets, in bytes. Below
  131,072 (128 KiB) is a compile error when it is a constant (NL2584) and
  stops the program when it is computed.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="ThreadScope">

a new scope of its own, joined when the block ends.

</scalar-field>

## Classes

### AtomicI32

An `i32` that a scope's tasks and a parallel body may update together
(docs/LANGUAGE.md, "Atomics"). Each method is one indivisible operation:
natively the compiler emits each body itself, as a sequentially consistent
`load atomic`, `store atomic`, `atomicrmw` or `cmpxchg` on `value`
(docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md, "Atomics"), and what is written below is the meaning,
which is what runs under Node. `add` and `sub` wrap at 32 bits, as the
native instruction does; `add`, `sub`, `min`, `max` and `exchange` answer
the value before the update, and `compareExchange` the value it saw.

It reaches a task by the routes a `Mutex` does, and a parallel body through
a capture; its value is named only through these methods. Results that do
not depend on the order the updates land in need the updates to commute,
which the checker does not prove.

```ts
class AtomicI32
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new AtomicI32(value: i32)` | An atomic holding `value`. |
| `add(delta: i32): i32` | Adds `delta`, wrapping, and answers the value before. |
| `compareExchange(expected: i32, desired: i32): i32` | Sets the value to `desired` if it is `expected`, and answers the value it saw. |
| `exchange(value: i32): i32` | Sets the value to `value` and answers the value before. |
| `load(): i32` | The value. |
| `max(value: i32): i32` | Keeps the larger of the value and `value`, and answers the value before. |
| `min(value: i32): i32` | Keeps the smaller of the value and `value`, and answers the value before. |
| `store(value: i32): void` | Sets the value to `value`. |
| `sub(delta: i32): i32` | Subtracts `delta`, wrapping, and answers the value before. |

### AtomicI64

An `i64` that a scope's tasks and a parallel body may update together
(docs/LANGUAGE.md, "Atomics"). Each method is one indivisible operation:
natively the compiler emits each body itself, as a sequentially consistent
`load atomic`, `store atomic`, `atomicrmw` or `cmpxchg` on `value`
(docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md, "Atomics"), and what is written below is the meaning,
which is what runs under Node. Node holds it as a `number`, so `add` and
`sub` are `+` and `-` there, and it agrees with native while values stay
within ±2^53; wrapping at 2^63 is native-only, the same limit as every `i64`.
`add`, `sub`, `min`, `max` and `exchange` answer the value before the
update, and `compareExchange` the value it saw.

It reaches a task by the routes a `Mutex` does, and a parallel body through
a capture; its value is named only through these methods. Results that do
not depend on the order the updates land in need the updates to commute,
which the checker does not prove.

```ts
class AtomicI64
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new AtomicI64(value: i64)` | An atomic holding `value`. |
| `add(delta: i64): i64` | Adds `delta` and answers the value before; natively the sum wraps at 64 bits. |
| `compareExchange(expected: i64, desired: i64): i64` | Sets the value to `desired` if it is `expected`, and answers the value it saw. |
| `exchange(value: i64): i64` | Sets the value to `value` and answers the value before. |
| `load(): i64` | The value. |
| `max(value: i64): i64` | Keeps the larger of the value and `value`, and answers the value before. |
| `min(value: i64): i64` | Keeps the smaller of the value and `value`, and answers the value before. |
| `store(value: i64): void` | Sets the value to `value`. |
| `sub(delta: i64): i64` | Subtracts `delta` and answers the value before; natively the difference wraps at 64 bits. |

### Channel

A channel of scalars or strings between a scope's tasks (docs/wp29-thread-surface.md
§4.4); a string is copied out of the sender's arena at `send` and into the
receiver's at the loop: `send` from the tasks that produce, `for (const x of ch)` in the one
that consumes, or in the parent once the scope has joined.

<scalar-code-group>

```ts example.ts
const ch = new Channel<i32>()
{
  using s = scope()
  s.spawn(produce, new Pipe(ch, 100), done, 0) // every sender first
  s.spawn(consume, new Pipe(ch, 0), sums, 0)   // then the one receiver
}
```

</scalar-code-group>

Nobody closes a channel: it closes when its scope has started to join and
every task that may send on it has returned (docs/LANGUAGE.md, "Channels").

**What is written here is the meaning under Node**, where a scope's tasks run
one at a time at their spawns: `send` pushes onto `queue`, and a loop takes
values off its front until it is empty. That is correct because every
sender is spawned before the receiver, so every sender has run by the time
the receiver's loop starts. Natively the compiler writes `send` and the loop
itself (`src/emit-parallel.ts`), onto a buffer the runtime keeps outside
every arena behind `state`, and the loop waits while the channel is empty
and still open.

```ts
class Channel<T>
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new Channel<T>()` | An empty channel, open until its scope joins. |
| `[Symbol.iterator](): ChannelWalk<T>` | What `for (const x of ch)` asks for under Node: a walk that takes each value as it reaches it, so a second loop over the channel finds it empty, as it does natively. |
| `send(x: T): void` | Hand `x` to the receiver. It never waits: a channel holds as many values as are sent. |

### Mutex

A lock that owns its data (docs/wp29-thread-surface.md §4.3). The data is
reachable only through the guard `lock()` answers, bound by `using`, so no
path to it skips the lock: `new Mutex<Hist>(new Hist())` takes a fresh
value, and `using g = m.lock()` is the only way to read or write it.

Under Node a scope's tasks run one at a time, at their spawn, so `lock()`
answers the guard and waits for nothing: that is one of the orders the
native program can run its critical sections in, and a program whose
guarded updates commute prints the same either way.

```ts
class Mutex<T>
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new Mutex<T>(init: T)` | A free lock that owns `init`. |
| `lock(): MutexGuard<T>` | The guard over the data, for a `using` declaration: `using g = m.lock()`. Natively the call waits until the lock is free and takes it. |

### MutexGuard

What a `Mutex` hands out: its data, as `value`, for as long as the block of
the `using` declaration that took the lock (docs/LANGUAGE.md, "A lock that
owns its data"). A guard is only ever named as `g.value`, and `g.value`
only as the base of a field or element access, so nothing read through it
outlives the lock.

Each `Mutex` makes exactly one guard, when it is made, and every lock hands
out that one: taking the lock allocates nothing.

```ts
class MutexGuard<T>
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new MutexGuard<T>(value: T)` | A guard over `value`, with the lock free. `Mutex` makes its one guard with this. |
| `value: T` | The data the lock owns. |
| `[Symbol.dispose](): void` | What `using` calls when the guard's block ends. Natively the compiler emits the release itself at every exit of the block, and under Node nothing was taken, so there is nothing to give back. |

### ThreadScope

A scope of tasks, joined when the block that declares it ends
(docs/wp29-thread-surface.md §4.2). It is only ever made by `scope()` in a
`using` declaration, and only ever used as the receiver of `spawn`
(docs/LANGUAGE.md, "Scoped tasks"), so no task can outlive it.

```ts
class ThreadScope
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new ThreadScope()` |  |
| `[Symbol.dispose](): void` | What `using` calls when the block ends. Natively the compiler emits the join itself at every exit of the block, and under Node every task has already run by the time this is reached, so there is nothing left to do. |
| `spawn<A, R>(entry: (arg: A) => R, arg: A, dst: R[], at: i32): void` | Run `entry(arg)` on a thread of its own and store its answer in `dst[at]` when the scope closes. `at` is checked here, before the task is taken, and again when its answer is stored. |
| `spawnThunk<R>(entry: () => R): void` | `s.spawn(() => work(xs))` as the compiler reads it: run the arrow, whose captured `const` locals are its arguments, on a thread of its own when the scope closes, and store nothing. Only the compiler names this method, and a program that names it is refused as `spawnWith`'s is (NL2389). |
| `spawnWith<A, R>(entry: (arg: A) => R, arg: A): void` | `s.spawn(entry, arg)` as the compiler reads it: run `entry(arg)` on a thread of its own when the scope closes, and store nothing. `entry` answers `void`. Only the compiler names this method (see `slotWritten`): a scope is only ever the receiver of a `spawn` statement, so `s.spawnWith(...)` written in a program is refused by that rule (NL2389), as passing the scope would be. |
